This low neonatal mass is coupled with a relatively rapid growth trajectory, as juveniles must attain sufficient body size to exploit seasonal resource pulses in their semi-desert habitat. Adult females ultimately reach an asymptotic body mass of up to 130 grams [Wwi = up to 130 grams], although considerable intraspecific variation exists, with individuals ranging from 42 grams to 130 grams depending on local food availability and population density. The observed range in adult female mass has been linked to differences in habitat productivity across the species' distribution, with individuals from more mesic Mediterranean sites generally attaining larger body sizes than those from hyper-arid interior populations.

The respiratory quotient measured during these trials was consistent with lipid-based metabolism, as expected for a granivorous rodent relying heavily on seeds and stored grains through the dry season. These metabolic data provide a critical baseline for understanding the species' energetic requirements and its capacity to cope with seasonal food limitation.

Such a strategy is particularly advantageous in arid ecosystems where favorable breeding conditions are sporadic and unpredictable, allowing individuals that survive lean years to capitalize on episodic resource bonanzas.
